body.heading: Two explanations, one wing
paragraphs: A wing produces lift in two connected ways. Its curved top surface and slight upward tilt make air speed up as it passes over the top, and faster air presses down less hard, so the higher pressure underneath pushes the wing up.

At the same time, the wing deflects the passing air downward, like a hand angled out of a car window. Pushing air down creates an equal and opposite push upward on the wing. These are not rival theories: the pressure difference and the downward deflection are two descriptions of the same flow.

body.heading: What the wing needs to work
paragraphs: Lift depends on speed, air density and the wing's angle to the airflow, called the angle of attack. Tilting the wing up a little increases lift, which is why aircraft nose up slightly as they climb away from the runway.

There is a limit. Tilt too far — beyond roughly 15 degrees — and the airflow can no longer follow the top surface smoothly. It breaks away in turbulence, lift collapses, and the wing stalls, which pilots train to avoid and recover from.

body.heading: Lift at real-world scale
paragraphs: The effect has to be powerful: a loaded Boeing 737 weighs around 70 tonnes, and its two wings generate enough lift to hold all of that in the air. At cruising altitude the air is thin, so the aircraft flies fast — around 850 kilometres per hour — to keep the airflow, and therefore the lift, strong enough.

Flaps at the back of the wing extend and curve downward for takeoff and landing. They increase lift at low speeds, letting a heavy aircraft leave the ground — and return to it — at speeds a runway can handle.
